summary: Defines the DNSSEC Lookaside Validation resource record, for publishing DNSSEC trust anchors outside the DNS delegation chain. It is informational and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A side list of trusted keys kept off to the side for when the normal chain of trust is incomplete. It is no longer used.

subtitle: An alternative way to establish trust in DNS validation

tldr.problem: Some DNS zones cannot get their parent zones to publish DNSSEC delegation signer records, making it impossible to validate the zone with the normal chain of trust.
tldr.mechanism: DLV defines a new resource record type that lets domain owners publish DNSSEC trust anchors in a separate location outside the DNS delegation chain, accessible at known lookside validation points.
tldr.outcome: DLV provided a workaround for incomplete DNSSEC chains until all zones implemented signing. It was made historic in 2024 after DNSSEC deployment improved.

today: RFC 4431 is Historic. DNSSEC Lookaside Validation was replaced by improvements in DNSSEC deployment where parent zones now reliably publish delegation signer records.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates DNS data by building a chain of cryptographic signatures from a trusted root down through each zone. However, if a parent zone does not sign or refuses to publish delegation signer records for its children, validators cannot establish a chain of trust.

The DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) resource record provides an alternative: zone owners can publish their trust anchors outside the normal delegation chain in a lookaside database.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS normally proves websites are real by asking each level of authority. But some levels refused to say 'yes, that's real.' DLV let people prove it a different way.

sections.title: The DLV Resource Record
sections.content:
The DLV record has the same structure as the DS (Delegation Signer) resource record defined in RFC 4034. It uses the same algorithm and digest type registries as DS records. The DLV record is assigned DNS type code 32769. Unlike DS records, a DLV record appears in a lookaside database, not on a parent's side of a zone cut; it may appear at the apex of a zone itself.

Software using DLV records must authenticate them cryptographically to avoid spoofing. DNSSEC itself is typically used to authenticate the DLV records themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: A DLV record looks like a proof record but lives in a separate box instead of with the normal DNS. You have to check that the DLV record is real before you trust it.

sections.title: Historic Status
sections.content: RFC 4431 is now Historic. DLV provided a temporary solution for DNSSEC deployment gaps but became obsolete as DNSSEC adoption improved and parent zones began signing their delegations. Modern validators no longer need DLV, since the normal DNSSEC chain of trust is now available in most of the DNS tree.
sections.plainLanguage: This workaround was helpful when the normal proof system was incomplete. Now that everything works properly, this side box is no longer used.
